title: Why Do Bananas Get Brown Spots? 🍌
description:
Why do bananas get brown spots? Ethylene gas switches on ripening, chlorophyll breaks down, starch turns to sugar, and an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase turns tiny patches of aging peel brown, and under UV light each spot glows blue.

Sources:
https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/bananas-change-colour-upon-ripening.html
https://www.alimentarium.org/en/magazine/kitchen/bananas-sugar-and-starch
https://phys.org/news/2009-09-bananas-bad-blue-uv-light.html

Animated in the Kawaii Anime style.

topic: Why do bananas get brown spots?
script:
Why does a banana get brown spots?
You'd never guess it's on purpose.
It starts with a gas called ethylene.
The banana makes it all by itself,
and it flips ripening on like a switch.
First, the green chlorophyll in the peel breaks down,
so the yellow underneath finally shows.
Inside, starch turns into sugar.
Sugar can climb from about 1 percent to around 17.
Then the peel starts getting old.
Little clusters of cells shut down on schedule,
and an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase
links chemicals in the peel into brown pigment.
That's your spot.
And here's the wild part.
Under ultraviolet light,
each spot glows with a bright blue ring,
from leftover bits of chlorophyll.
So more spots usually means a sweeter banana.
Which one do you grab:
green, yellow, or totally spotty?
key_facts: Ethylene is the ripening hormone bananas make themselves (Science ABC)
Chlorophyll in the peel breaks down and starch turns into sugars (Science ABC)
Sugars rise from about 1.3% to about 17% as the fruit ripens (Alimentarium, plantain/ripe fruit figures)
Polyphenol oxidase polymerises phenols in the peel into brown pigment (Science ABC)
Each brown spot shows a blue halo under UV from chlorophyll breakdown products near dying tissue (phys.org 2009, Krautler & Turro, PNAS)
